name: Haiti
status_headline: TPS for Haiti has ended. As of September 3, 2026 nothing is holding it back.
in_sixty_seconds: TPS for Haiti is over. The government announced it in November 2025 and it took effect on February 3, 2026.
A judge paused it for a few months. That pause is gone — the Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 and the last protection lifted on August 5, 2026.
About 353,000 Haitians had TPS. Roughly 158,000 of them are in Florida.
Their work permits ended too. The date printed on the card does not matter; the card is only good as long as the status underneath it.
TPS never led to a green card. Anyone who has been waiting for it to turn into one was misinformed.
There may still be options — and losing TPS does not automatically close off asylum, which surprises almost everyone.
Their work permit, their protection from removal and their status all ended on the same day — but a case may still be possible, and speed matters.

timeline.event: Haiti designated for TPS after the January 12 earthquake.
Terminated. The termination was enjoined in litigation and never took effect.
DHS partially vacates the 2024 decision, cutting the 18-month extension to 12 months.
A federal court in New York holds the Secretary lacked authority to partially vacate a TPS designation.
timeline.cite: Haitian Evangelical Clergy Ass'n v. Trump, E.D.N.Y.

timeline.event: Five Haitian TPS holders sue over the termination.
DHS publishes the operative termination notice, effective February 3, 2026 at 11:59 p.m.
Judge Ana Reyes stays the termination, finding it was not the product of reasoned decision-making.
The Supreme Court grants certiorari before judgment.
The Supreme Court decides Mullin v. Doe, 6-3, holding that courts may not hear non-constitutional challenges to TPS terminations.
The Supreme Court's judgment issues — the last day court-ordered protection held.
The district court confirms its stay is no longer in effect. The equal protection claim remains pending.

notes.text: A further 18,068 people in that count had also been approved as lawful permanent residents, and so are not left without status by the termination.

by_state.label: Estimated Haitian TPS holders by state
by_state.caveat: No government agency publishes a state-by-state count. These are estimates from an advocacy organization, modeled from census survey data. Treat them as roughly right, not exact.

who_is_affected.heading: How many people, and where

what_termination_means.detail: Most people go back to having no status at all, and start building up unlawful presence. For someone who entered without being inspected, that is where they are now.
Work authorization came with the status, so it ended when the status did. Employers running E-Verify will see this. The expiration date printed on the card is not the real date.

what_termination_means.point: It was never going to become a green card.
what_termination_means.detail: DHS says it in the termination notice itself: granting TPS "does not result in or lead to lawful permanent resident status or any other immigration status." Say this gently. Some families have organized years around the opposite belief.

what_termination_means.point: But it did clear one hurdle quietly.
what_termination_means.detail: While they held TPS they counted as being in lawful status for one of the two green-card requirements. The other requirement — having been inspected and admitted — is the one TPS does not supply on its own.
If they left the country on Form I-512T and were admitted on the way back, that second requirement may be met. Ask. Write down the answer. Do not interpret it.

what_termination_means.point: The 60-day notice was not extra time.
what_termination_means.detail: The law requires at least 60 days between announcing a termination and it taking effect. That is a notice period. It never granted anyone more time to work or stay.

conditions.intro: Helpers get asked why someone will not just go home. This is what home looks like right now. These are UN, WHO and U.S. government figures. Where a bar covers only part of a year it is drawn striped, and it cannot be compared to the full years next to it.

metrics.label: People killed in violence
metrics.note: The UN started counting this way in 2022, so the chart starts there. One thing to keep straight: most of these deaths recently were not caused by gangs. In the first three months of 2026 the UN attributed 69 percent of casualties to security-force operations. Repeating the total without that gets the story wrong.

Half a year only. Sum of BINUH quarterly reports for Q1 (1,642) and Q2 (1,408). Do not compare to the full years above and do not annualize.

metrics.label: People forced from their homes, still inside Haiti
metrics.note: About 85 percent are not in camps — they are staying with relatives and neighbors. That is roughly one in eight people in the country.

metrics.label: Reported kidnappings
metrics.note: The UN says the real number is higher. Families often do not report a kidnapping and negotiate with the captors themselves.

points.text: Cholera has declined sharply. Haiti recorded 529 cases and 2 deaths between January 1 and May 31, 2026, against 3,664 suspected cases and 71 deaths in all of 2025.
Only about 10 percent of national health facilities with inpatient capacity are fully operational, and an estimated 40 percent of medical personnel have left the country.
6.4 million people in Haiti are assessed as needing humanitarian assistance in 2026, up from 6.0 million in 2025.

events.text: UN Security Council Resolution 2793 authorizes a Gang Suppression Force of up to 5,550 personnel and establishes a UN Support Office in Haiti.
Resolution 2814 renews the BINUH mandate to January 31, 2027.
The Transitional Presidential Council's mandate ends and the council is dissolved, leaving Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime as the sole executive authority.
The UN Support Office becomes fully operational and the first Gang Suppression Force troops arrive. The Kenyan contingent that formed the bulk of the predecessor mission departs during April.

The Gang Suppression Force formally begins operations in limited capacity. By July 8 it stood at 1,083 military personnel, contributed by Chad, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka — roughly a fifth of its authorized ceiling.
The electoral council sets a first round of national elections for December 13, 2026, with a runoff on February 21, 2027 — the first national vote in a decade.
events.flag: Confirmed through Security Council Report; the electoral council's own calendar was not opened directly.

status_sub: If someone tells you they have TPS from Haiti, they no longer do, and their work permit ended with it.

what_happened.heading: What happened, briefly
paragraphs: Haiti has had TPS on and off since the 2010 earthquake, and continuously since 2021. In July 2024 it was extended for eighteen months. In February 2025 the government cut that extension short, and a federal court in New York later held it did not have the authority to do that.

In November 2025 the government terminated the designation outright, effective February 3, 2026. It said letting Haitians remain was contrary to the national interest, pointing to border encounters, a visa overstay rate near 25 percent, and a finding that Haiti lacks a functioning central authority able to share law-enforcement information.

Five Haitian TPS holders sued. On February 2, 2026, the day before it was to take effect, a federal judge in Washington paused the termination, finding it was not the product of reasoned decision-making.

The government appealed and the Supreme Court took the case directly. On June 25, 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, it ruled 6 to 3 that courts may not hear this kind of challenge to a TPS termination at all — the statute forecloses it. Three justices disagreed. The judgment issued on July 27 and the pause was formally lifted on August 5, 2026.

One claim is still alive in the lower court, arguing the decision was racially discriminatory, which the Supreme Court did not foreclose. It has not been decided, and it is not protecting anyone right now.

sources.org: Haitian Evangelical Clergy Ass'n v. Trump (E.D.N.Y.)

also_ask.heading: Also ask: did they come in on CHNV parole?
also_ask.body: Separately from TPS, more than 200,000 Haitians entered between 2022 and 2025 through a sponsorship program known as CHNV parole. That program was terminated in March 2025 and existing grants ended that April, along with the work permits attached to them. Someone may have had one, the other, or both — and the answer changes what they can do next.

critical_questions.heading: Two questions worth asking
critical_questions.lede: Both of these are specific to people who held TPS, and both are routinely missed. Ask them, write the answers down, and make sure the lawyer hears them. Do not try to work out what they mean.

items.title: Ask whether they ever travelled on a TPS travel document.
items.body: This is the single question most likely to change someone's case. Many people who had TPS first entered the country without being inspected at a border post. That blocks them from applying for a green card from inside the United States, even if they marry a U.S. citizen. But since July 2022, a TPS holder who travelled abroad on Form I-512T and was let back in is treated as having been inspected and admitted. That one trip can turn an impossible case into a workable one.
items.why: Ask it, write down the answer, and make sure the lawyer hears it. Do not try to work out what it means.

source.org: USCIS Policy Alert, TPS and Adjustment of Status

items.title: Losing TPS does not automatically close off asylum.
items.body: Asylum normally has to be filed within one year of arriving, and people who have been here a decade assume that door shut long ago. But the regulation lists holding TPS as an extraordinary circumstance that excuses a late filing, as long as they file within a reasonable period after it ends. Many people do not know this, and some are told the opposite.
items.why: The word that matters is soon. A reasonable period is not measured in years.

orgs.heading: Organizations serving Haitians
orgs.note: These serve the Haitian community, most of them in South Florida where the majority of Haitian TPS holders live. Inclusion is not an endorsement. Details change, so each links to the organization's own page rather than repeating a phone number here.

list.name: Catholic Legal Services, Archdiocese of Miami
list.what: Nonprofit law firm representing low-income immigrants. Work permits, applications and removal defense. Formed in part from the G.W.L. Haitian legal services project.

list.name: Americans for Immigrant Justice
list.what: Nonprofit law firm doing direct representation, impact litigation and advocacy. Recruits pro bono attorneys.

list.name: Haitian Bridge Alliance
list.what: Haiti-focused advocacy organization providing pro bono legal support and a community hotline. Active on Haiti TPS.

list.name: Sant La Haitian Neighborhood Center
list.what: Community center serving South Florida's Haitian-American community, with Creole-language programming and a TPS resource center.
list.cost: Not stated on the organization's site
list.flag: Whether this is direct legal representation or referral is not stated publicly. Call before relying on it.

list.name: Family Action Network Movement (FANM)
list.what: Community organization with immigration, citizenship and policy programs, adult education and housing advocacy.
list.cost: Not stated on the organization's site
list.flag: Legal scope and cost are not stated publicly. Call before relying on it.

list.name: Florida Immigrant Coalition
list.what: Grassroots coalition running legal services, advocacy and a free hotline.
